extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (scientists, researchers, librarians, and informed public interested in science books, reports, and correspondence)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and expectations that Nature reviewers and correspondents apply when evaluating scientific books, technical treatises, instruments, and letters; includes editorial submission policies and experimental/technical standards discussed in reviews and correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial submission policy and correspondence rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Editor does not hold himself responsible for opinions expressed by correspondents; will not return or correspond about rejected manuscripts; no notice taken of anonymous communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors submitting letters or manuscripts should not expect editorial correspondence about rejections, should sign submissions (anonymous communications will not be noticed), and should not regard the Editor as endorsing views published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and simplicity of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental conceptions (e.g., energy, entropy, temperature) should be given in their simplest form and clearly explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good introductory treatise should present core concepts accessibly (example: Bryan's treatment of energy, entropy, temperature) and provide a general summary; unclear or overly terse statements may require longer, more satisfactory summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original contribution / incorporation of original research
rubrics_metrics.description: A work should not merely follow beaten tracks but should present results of original research where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers value when an author brings fresh perspectives or original results rather than repeating standard material; Prof. Bryan is commended for including original research in a treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of theoretical definitions where required
rubrics_metrics.description: Key quantities (e.g., absolute temperature, entropy) should be defined theoretically when appropriate and with reference to standard constructions (e.g., Carnot cycle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical definitions may be necessary even if they are not directly measurable; explicitly state such definitions and their intended theoretical role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical rigor and suitability of definitions to physical reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions (e.g., density, temperature at a point) must be logically defensible and applicable to the physical medium considered (continuous vs molecular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where continuum definitions fail for discrete molecular media, give logical alternative formulations and practical assumptions (e.g., averaging over an element of volume large compared with molecular dimensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness of explanation and justification of assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficult or potentially questionable principles (e.g., claims about irreversibility and entropy gain in diffusion) should be more fully explained and justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid leaving contentious statements unsupported; reviewers expect adequate discussion, justification, and acknowledgment of limitations or counterarguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive and balanced coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: A handbook or general work should be remarkably complete and well balanced, covering final products, forms, dynamics, distribution, and causes in reasonable proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good handbooks trace topics from end-products back to causes and give balanced treatment across subtopics (example: Mercalli's volcano treatise praised for completeness and balance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair presentation of alternative theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should state alternative explanations fairly without unduly pressing a favored theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present competing hypotheses candidly and weigh alternatives; do not overcommit to unproven theories—state them and their limits (Mercalli's book treated alternatives fairly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and usefulness of illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations should be numerous, excellent, and serve to elucidate the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality plates, drawings, and photographs increase a work's value; technical illustrations should support and clarify descriptions (volcanoes and shaft-sinking reviews emphasize good illustrations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of level to intended audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The material should be pitched at the appropriate level (elementary, advanced student, or experienced practitioner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers comment on whether a book is for elementary students, advanced students, or practitioners (e.g., shaft sinking book 'not a book for elementary students' but recommended for advanced students and experienced engineers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of bibliographies, indices, and references
rubrics_metrics.description: Works should include bibliographies and indices and, where helpful, suggestions for further reading (e.g., lists at chapter ends).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The absence of bibliographies or indices is noted as a deficiency; adding references or chapter-reading lists improves utility for readers and students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of content and editorial/translation quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Text must be free from spelling errors, mistranslations, and factual inaccuracies; terminology must be correct (e.g., correct names, taxonomies, chemical terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor translation and factual mistakes undermine a book's value (the toxins book is criticized for many spelling/translation errors and incorrect statements); careful editing and expert translation are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate depth and focus for subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A book attempting to survey a broad domain must provide sufficient depth; superficial, sketchy treatments are inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-compressing large subjects into too few pages; where breadth is attempted, ensure sufficient detail or restrict scope to provide meaningful coverage (the toxins book criticized for being superficial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical utility and experience-based guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical directions and management guidance should be based on long experience and clearly expressed for users (e.g., greenhouse management).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers appreciate simple, clear, experience-based instructions that make cultivation or practice achievable; practical examples and long-tested techniques are valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic and functional quality of plates and photographs
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs and colored plates should be both attractive and effective; poor-quality plates reduce usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality photographs can be very effective and engaging, whereas unattractive colored plates detract; choose plates that are both informative and visually acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical drawing scale and detail for engineering works
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale, dimensioned drawings enhance the value of technical descriptions (e.g., shaft designs) and aid selection of methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For engineering texts, include clear, dimensioned figures to illustrate methods; such drawings help practitioners select appropriate techniques for difficult cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical applicability and guidance for method selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical treatises should facilitate the selection of the best method for a particular case by reviewing available options and their contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide comparative descriptions, use-cases, successes/failures, and conditions under which particular methods are preferred (shaft sinking review praises a review that helps select methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental rigor: purification, controls, and contamination avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments must control sources of error (e.g., accidental introduction of salts), start with purified materials, and guard against contamination to yield conclusive results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments with appropriate purification, controls, and awareness of accidental impurities; repeat and confirm with purified samples (radium correspondence stresses purified uranium salts and possible contamination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper interpretation of quantitative significance and replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should assess whether results are quantitatively significant and be cautious in drawing genetic or causal conclusions without robust evidence and replication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish qualitative observations from quantitatively significant findings; replication by other investigators (or failure to replicate) must inform interpretation (discussion of radium production emphasizes quantitative significance and replication concerns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument performance criteria: accuracy, readability, durability, and cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruments intended as standards should provide exact readings, adequate bore and column diameter for clear readings, verniers capable of fine resolution, durable construction (bronzed/lacquered metal, silvered scales), useful mounting and reflectors, and moderate cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or producing scientific instruments (example: 'Student's' Standard Barometer), ensure measurement precision (vernier/readability), robust construction and finish, appropriate mounting/adjustment features, and balance accuracy with affordability for intended users (students, schools, observatories).
